vignette:
Imran was a 58-year-old South Asian plumber who had lived in the United States for most of his adult life, married for thirty-two years, and known in his neighborhood as the man who could fix a burst pipe without making a fuss. That steadiness had been shattered years earlier during a terrorist attack at a crowded public transit station, when armed men forced people to the floor and shouted orders over the noise and panic. He still described the scene easily, almost too easily, as if the facts came out in a clean list, yet he also said that when he tried to place the events in order, the memory refused to settle. Certain fragments came unbidden: a voice barking commands, the smell of dust and hot metal, the crush of bodies, his own hands obeying before he had time to think. He had come to believe that what he did in those moments went against who he was, and that he should have done more to stop what happened; he spoke of that with a heavy, unyielding shame, insisting that he would never forgive himself. He also felt he had lost his connection to his community and culture, as though something between him and the people who once anchored him had been cut away. Those beliefs made the memory return with extra force, as if each replay were proof that he had failed in a way that could not be undone. They also made ordinary cues more charged for him: a harsh tone, a crowded platform, even a date on the calendar could snag his attention and feel like a warning he could not dismiss.

Since then, Imran had found that the anniversary of the attack could turn an ordinary week unstable. In the days around it, a related voice on television or in the street - a tone too close to the men who shouted that day - could pull the memory into his mind before he wanted it there, and once it arrived it brought the whole scene back in broken pieces. The more those reminders were around him, the more his body read them as signs that danger was close, and he would catch himself tense, looking over his shoulder as if something terrible were about to happen. At the same time, hearing that sort of voice or noticing the anniversary coming up could drag him straight back into the station, with the dust, the orders, and the crush of bodies feeling immediate again rather than remembered. He could talk about what happened very easily, but saying it aloud did not make it less vivid; if anything, the telling seemed to sharpen the details and leave him more convinced that he had failed himself. His shame and sense of having betrayed his values made the memory stick harder, and the more it came back, the more he judged himself for not having acted differently. That self-judgment then fed into the way he moved through the world: he became wary of being forced to do anything, and even a supervisor's blunt instruction on a job site could leave him bristling, as if another order were about to strip away his control. The memory would often surface first, and once it did, he found himself scanning the environment for anything that resembled that day - voices, crowds, a tone of command - and those details were harder to ignore after the image had already come back. In that way, the recollection kept seeding new reminders, and each reminder made it easier for him to feel cornered all over again. The more he felt cornered, the more the memory seemed to rush in again, with the same feeling of submission and helplessness he hated in himself. That constant sense of threat also hardened the harsh conclusions he drew about himself: if his body was still reacting like this, he took it as proof that he was weak and had failed to protect himself or others. The fear in his daily life gradually became the most convincing evidence for his self-blame.

In the months after the attack, his body began to behave as though danger were still near. He often reacted as if something terrible was about to happen even when nothing was actually wrong, scanning rooms and hesitating at doorways. He woke in the night to check whether he was safe, walking softly through the house so he would not disturb his wife, and at work he found it hard to concentrate on measurements or repairs because part of him remained on alert for the next threat. Living at that pitch of danger, he started to read more and more cues as if they carried a message, so a raised voice in a customer's hallway or a crowded station platform on the way to a plumbing call could set off the same surge of alarm. The constant sense that something might happen also seemed to confirm the harsh conclusions he had about himself, leaving him more convinced that he was weak for still feeling this frightened. Those moments of false alarm did not stay abstract for long; they made him more likely to notice anything that resembled that day, and once he noticed, he moved to avoid it. He steered clear of crowded stations, avoided situations where someone might order him around, and grew tense around voices that sounded similar to the one he remembered. Even his routes to plumbing jobs changed so he would not pass the place where an anniversary display had been set up the previous year, since that date had become a time when his mind and body seemed to expect danger.

Imran's fear of danger and loss of control and the reminders that set him off had become inseparable. When he woke already braced for trouble, the force of that threat made him more vigilant about voices, anniversaries, and any situation in which he might be made to comply. When the memory intruded, it did not remain in the past; it made him feel unsafe in the present and then pushed him back into shame and self-blame. His wife had begun to notice that he was more withdrawn, quicker to startle, and less willing to attend family gatherings, especially around community events that once mattered to him. He finally sought help after a night of waking repeatedly to check locks and windows, exhausted and ashamed, and after missing a day of work because he could not keep his mind on the job. What frightened him most was that he might stay trapped in this state, always reacting as if danger were still there; what he hoped for was to sleep through the night, return to his work without losing his focus, and feel part of his community again without the attack taking over every reminder of it.
